:::{#thm-uc-undecidable}
#### The diagonal problem is undecidable

The [diagonal problem](#def-diagonal-problem) UC is [undecidable](#def-decidable)
[@arora2009computational, section 1.5].

:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose a [Turing machine](models-of-computation.qmd#def-turing-machine) $M$ [decides](models-of-computation.qmd#def-tm-computes) UC,
and let $w$ be a [description](models-of-computation.qmd#def-tm-description) of $M$,
so that $M_w = M$.
Then $M$ [halts](models-of-computation.qmd#def-turing-machine) on $w$
with [output](models-of-computation.qmd#def-turing-machine) $1$ or $0$.

- If $M(w) = 1$, then $w \in \text{UC}$, because $M$ decides UC.
  By @def-diagonal-problem, $w \in \text{UC}$ means $M_w(w) \ne 1$,
  that is, $M(w) \ne 1$, a contradiction.
- If $M(w) = 0$, then $w \notin \text{UC}$, because $M$ decides UC.
  By @def-diagonal-problem, $w \notin \text{UC}$ means $M_w(w) = 1$,
  that is, $M(w) = 1$, a contradiction.

Both cases are impossible, so no Turing machine decides UC.

:::
